lineage_context.teaching_goal: Teach the cruciform flower, tetradynamous stamens and replum-bearing fruit as the core mustard-family architecture, then compare directly with Cleomaceae.

project_scope.selection_mode: Central Texas family-first recognition module across thirteen project-pool genera
project_scope.note: The pool includes both native and introduced mustards and several legacy generic names. Species-level taxonomy/range stays in separate workflows.

family_diagnostics.where_to_look_first: LOOK HERE FIRST: if flowers are present, count stamens before trusting the four-petal cross—Brassicaceae typically has 6 in a 4-long + 2-short tetradynamous set. If fruit is present, split one open: two valves should leave a persistent replum/septum framework. Fruit architecture is the strongest tie-breaker when flowers are tiny, reduced, or already gone.
family_diagnostics.vegetative: Mostly annual, biennial or perennial herbs; leaves usually alternate and without stipules, often forming a basal rosette. Mustard oils commonly produce a pungent odor or taste, but do not rely on tasting plants.
family_diagnostics.reproductive: Usually 4 free sepals + 4 free, commonly clawed petals; stamens typically 6 and tetradynamous (4 longer inner + 2 shorter outer). The ovary is superior and bicarpellate; a false septum (replum/septum framework) partitions the developing fruit. Important exceptions exist: petals may be reduced/absent and stamen number can depart from six, so fruit should arbitrate doubtful plants.
family_diagnostics.fruit: Usually silique/silicle architecture: two valves detach from a persistent replum/frame, commonly exposing the septum and seeds. Long-vs-short fruit proportions help route genera, but some local/encounter mustards have strongly modified or indehiscent fruits, so 'must have a normal pod' is unsafe.
family_diagnostics.field_tip: Four cross-like petals gets attention; 4-long + 2-short stamens and a replum-bearing fruit confirm the family.

visual_lesson.teaching_order: flower face → 4-long + 2-short stamen map → ovary/replum cutaway → mature fruit opening → fruit-shape genus routing → Cleomaceae/Fabaceae/Caryophyllaceae tie-breakers
visual_lesson.intro: Do not stop at 'four petals like a cross.' For a field-proof mustard ID, make the learner prove either the tetradynamous stamen pattern or the replum-bearing fruit—and ideally both.

steps.title: 1 · See the cross-shaped flower
steps.look_for: Four free petals arranged in a cross, with four sepals beneath.
steps.why_it_matters: The old name Cruciferae literally points to this cross-shaped corolla.

steps.title: 2 · Count 4 long + 2 short stamens
steps.look_for: Six stamens with four conspicuously longer than the other two.
steps.why_it_matters: Tetradynamous stamens are one of the strongest mustard-family confirmation characters.

steps.title: 3 · Open the fruit and find the replum
steps.look_for: Two valves fall away while a central frame/septum remains with the seeds attached.
steps.why_it_matters: The fruit architecture separates Brassicaceae from superficially similar dry pods.

steps.title: 4 · Learn silique vs silicle as shape, not a new fruit type
steps.photo_role: long narrow vs short broad mustard fruits
steps.look_for: Both use the same replum-bearing architecture; 'silique' is elongate, 'silicle' is relatively short/broad.
steps.why_it_matters: Fruit shape is extremely useful for narrowing mustard genera.

steps.title: 5 · Use the fruit to enter the genus
steps.look_for: Lepidium and many Draba use shorter silicles; Sisymbrium and Descurainia commonly make long narrow siliques.
steps.why_it_matters: Once family is known, fruit proportions often beat flowers for genus work.

comparisons.title: Brassicaceae vs Cleomaceae
comparisons.brassicaceae: Usually 6 stamens in a 4-long + 2-short tetradynamous set; flower commonly regular/cruciform; leaves usually simple or divided without the locally common 3-foliolate Cleomaceae look.
comparisons.other: Local Cleomaceae commonly has more strongly exserted, non-tetradynamous stamens (often far more than 6), more asymmetric flowers, and often 3-foliolate/glandular foliage.
comparisons.tie_breaker: Count stamens and compare their lengths before using petal color or pod shape.

comparisons.title: Brassicaceae vs Fabaceae
comparisons.brassicaceae: Two valves separate from a persistent replum/septum framework; seeds remain associated with that central framework.
comparisons.other: A legume develops from one carpel and lacks the mustard replum; when it opens, the pod wall splits along its sutures rather than leaving a mustard-style central frame.
comparisons.tie_breaker: Open a mature fruit. Replum present = mustard architecture; one-carpel legume = Fabaceae.

comparisons.title: Brassicaceae vs Caryophyllaceae
comparisons.brassicaceae: Leaves usually alternate; fruit typically silique/silicle with replum.
comparisons.other: Leaves usually opposite at conspicuous/swollen nodes; flowers commonly 5-merous; fruit commonly a capsule opening by teeth/valves rather than a mustard replum.
comparisons.tie_breaker: When flowers are tiny, node/leaf arrangement plus mature fruit is safer than petal count alone.

comparisons.title: Brassicaceae vs Papaveraceae
comparisons.brassicaceae: Usually no conspicuous colored latex; stamens commonly 6 tetradynamous; replum-bearing fruit.
comparisons.other: Poppies commonly have conspicuous latex and numerous stamens; capsules do not use the mustard 2-valve + replum plan.
comparisons.tie_breaker: Numerous stamens/latex point away from Brassicaceae; confirm with fruit architecture.

visual_lesson.caveat: Not every Brassicaceae flower has all four petals or exactly six stamens, and not every fruit is a textbook dehiscent silique. Use the whole suite rather than one rule.
exceptions: Petals can be reduced or absent; a four-petal cross is a common pattern, not an absolute gate.
Stamen number can vary; tetradynamy is highly useful when present but should be paired with fruit on atypical plants.
Rapistrum-type encounter taxa can have jointed/beaked indehiscent fruit rather than a textbook opening silique.
Aquatic Nasturtium can look vegetatively unlike a dry-ground mustard; use flowers and fruit rather than habitat gestalt.
Legacy names such as Lesquerella belong to taxonomy routing, not family recognition; do not reopen accepted-name decisions here.

routing_key: Short/broad or strongly flattened fruit → check Lepidium, Draba, Capsella and other silicle-bearing genera; use notch, hairs and fruit outline next.
Long narrow fruit → compare Sisymbrium, Descurainia, Arabis, Streptanthus, Nerisyrenia, Diplotaxis and Sibara; then use leaf dissection, pedicel angle, fruit compression and flower details.
Jointed/beaked or indehiscent fruit → route early to Rapistrum-type exceptions rather than forcing a normal silique key.
Aquatic/emergent plant with pinnate leaves → check Nasturtium before terrestrial mustard routes.
